function.description: Executes a system-level command using os.system() on Windows operating systems. It can execute single or multiple commands chained with '&&'. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

command.description: The system command to be executed. To execute multiple commands, separate them with '&&'. For example, 'dir && echo done'.

message.content:
I don’t have a way to probe your connection from here, but you can quickly find out your current download/upload speeds yourself. Here are a few reliable methods:

---

## 1. **Web‑based Speed Test (easiest)**  
1. Open a browser and go to one of the following sites:  
   * [speedtest.net](https://www.speedtest.net)  
   * [fast.com](https://fast.com) (Netflix’s test)  
   * [speedof.me](https://speedof.me)  
2. Click “Go” or “Start” and let the test run.  
3. The page will display:
   * **Download speed** (Mbps or Mbit/s)  
   * **Upload speed** (Mbps or Mbit/s)  
   * **Ping** (latency in ms)

These sites automatically pick the nearest server, so the results are usually representative of what you’ll experience in real‑world usage.

---

## 2. **Command‑Line Speed Test (for Linux/macOS/Windows)**  

If you prefer a terminal or want to script the test, you can use the open‑source `speedtest-cli` tool.

### Install `speedtest-cli`

| OS | Command |
|----|---------|
| **Linux** (Debian/Ubuntu) | `sudo apt-get install speedtest-cli` |
| **Linux** (Fedora/CentOS) | `sudo dnf install speedtest-cli` |
| **macOS** (Homebrew) | `brew install speedtest-cli` |
| **Windows** (PowerShell) | `pip install speedtest-cli` (requires Python) |

> **Tip:** If you’re on Windows and don’t have Python, you can install it from the Microsoft Store or use the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL).

### Run the Test

```bash
speedtest
```

The output will look something like this:

```
Testing from Your ISP (Your City)...
Retrieving speedtest.net configuration...
Testing download speed........................................
Download:  85.23 Mbit/s
Testing upload speed..........................................
Upload:    12.45 Mbit/s
```

---

## 3. **Using the Built‑In Windows Speed Test (Windows 10/11)**

Windows 10/11 includes a built‑in speed test in the Settings app:

1. Open **Settings** → **Network & Internet** → **Status**.  
2. Scroll down to the “Internet speed” section.  
3. Click **Run a speed test**.  
4. The test will run and display the results.

---

## 4. **Router/Modem Web Interface**

Many consumer routers have a “Status” or “Diagnostics” page that shows current throughput. Log into your router’s admin panel (usually `192.168.1.1` or `192.168.0.1`) and look for a “Speed Test” or “Status” tab. This can give you a quick snapshot of the link between your router and the ISP.

---

## 5. **Mobile Apps**

If you’re on a phone, there are many free apps that perform speed tests:

* **Speedtest by Ookla** (Android & iOS)  
* **Fast.com** (Android & iOS)  
* **OpenSignal** (Android & iOS)

Just open the app, tap “Go,” and wait for the results.

---

### Quick Summary

| Method | Pros | Cons |
|--------|------|------|
| Web site | Very easy, no setup | Requires a browser |
| `speedtest-cli` | Scriptable, CLI | Needs installation |
| Windows Settings | Built‑in | Only on Windows 10/11 |
| Router UI | Shows link to ISP | Depends on router firmware |
| Mobile app | Portable | Requires a phone |

Pick the one that fits your workflow. Once you run a test, you’ll know your current download/upload speeds and latency, which you can compare against your ISP’s advertised plan. If the numbers are consistently lower than promised, you might want to contact your ISP or troubleshoot further.
